questions.topic: Standalone, market and investment value in a takeover
questions.syllabus_objective: Introduction to valuation: users and uses, bases of value (market value vs investment value), price vs value
questions.stem: Kappa SpA generates a free cash flow from operations of €36m a year, flat forever. Its WACC is 9% and its net debt is €100m. It has 30 million shares trading at €11.00. Omega, an industrial buyer, expects after-tax synergies of €8m a year, starting next year and flat forever, discounted at the same 9%, and needs €25m of one-off integration costs today.

source.file: Slides/Corporate Valuation - AY 26-27 - Lectures 1-2 - Introduction - v3.pdf
source.location: slides 39–44 (bases of value and the apartment example)
source.label: INFERENCE

subquestions.prompt: Compute Kappa's standalone equity value, Omega's investment value for 100% of Kappa's equity, and Omega's NPV if it pays €12.50 per share. Round to one decimal.

Omega now expects the synergies to grow at 2% a year from the first-year €8m (other inputs unchanged). Kappa's board will reject any offer below a 15% premium on the €11.00 share price. Is there a price per share that works for both sides? Give the range.

answer_key.answer: Yes: from €12.65 (board floor) to €12.98 (Omega's maximum) per share.

error_tags.trap: a: integration cost of 25 left out (NPV +13.9)
a: market cap 330 used as the standalone value
a: EV used instead of equity value
b: synergies valued as a flat perpetuity (max €12.13, no deal)
b: 15% premium applied to standalone €10.00 instead of the market price

mark_scheme: [a] Steps: (1) standalone EV = 36 / 9% = 400.0; (2) standalone equity = 400.0 − 100 = 300.0; (3) PV of synergies = 8 / 9% = 88.9; (4) less integration cost 25; (5) investment value = 300.0 + 88.9 − 25 = 363.9; (6) offer = 12.50 × 30 = 375.0; (7) NPV = 363.9 − 375.0 = -11.1: at €12.50 Omega destroys value.
Second route for [a]: (36 + 8)/9% − 25 − 100 = 363.9. The market value (€330m) is a third basis, above standalone because the market prices in some expectations; it is not the investment value.

[b] Steps: (1) growing synergies: 8 / (9% − 2%) = 114.3; (2) investment value = 300.0 + 114.3 − 25 = 389.3; (3) maximum per share = 389.3 / 30 = 12.98; (4) board floor = 11.00 × 1.15 = 12.65; (5) compare: floor < maximum; (6) so a deal zone exists; (7) range €12.65–€12.98.
How to write it: name each basis of value (standalone, market, investment) before computing; the offer price is not a value.
Where marks are lost: dropping the integration cost, using market cap as standalone value, forgetting net debt, or valuing growing synergies as flat.

citations.quote: The investment value (for A) is therefore - €k 10 + €k 20 ÷ 10% = €k 190
It includes the benefits, e.g. expected synergies, that the current owner or a potential investor can generate
Price is not a synonym of value

questions.topic: Three DCF models, one value, then a debt-funded buyback
questions.syllabus_objective: DCF valuation: capital structure theory (MM with taxes), APV, equity-side DCF and WACC
questions.stem: Rho SpA has a constant EBIT of €150m in perpetuity, maintenance investment only (no growth), an unlevered cost of equity of 11%, perpetual debt of €400m at a 5% interest rate equal to its cost of debt, and a 25% tax rate. Tax shields are as risky as debt.

source.file: Slides/Corporate Valuation - AY 26-27 - Lecture 3 - DCF Valuation - v6.pdf
source.location: slides 7–16 (MM with taxes, APV, equity-side DCF, WACC example)
source.label: INFERENCE

subquestions.prompt: Value Rho with the APV method, then compute its levered cost of equity (MM 2) and WACC, and show that the equity-side DCF gives the same equity value.

Rho borrows another €200m (perpetual, same 5% cost) and uses all of it to buy back shares at a fair price. Before the deal there are 50 million shares. What is the price per share after the buyback, and the new WACC?

error_tags.trap: a: EV = VU only
a: D/E at book instead of market values
a: FCFE = FCFO − interest
b: price computed from the old equity value (€14.45)
b: post-deal equity divided by 50m shares

mark_scheme: [b] Steps: (1) new debt 600; (2) VTS = 600 × 25% = 150.0; (3) EV = 1172.7; (4) the extra tax shield of 50.0 goes to today's shareholders on announcement; (5) price = (722.7 + 50.0) / 50 = 15.45; (6) shares bought = 200 / 15.45 = 12.94m; (7) remaining 37.06m; (8) equity after = 1172.7 − 600 = 572.7 = 15.45 × 37.06m (check); (9) WACC = 112.5 / 1172.7 = 9.59%.
How to write it: state MM 1 (EV rises by D·t) and MM 2 (kEL rises with market D/E) in one line each, then compute.
Where marks are lost: book D/E in MM 2, FCFE without the tax shield, pricing the buyback at the old €14.45, or dividing post-deal equity by 50m shares.

citations.quote: Modigliani & Miller 1: as debt increases, enterprise value increases thanks to an increase in the future tax shields (TS)
Modigliani & Miller 2: as debt increases, the cost of equity moves UP from the unlevered case:
The D/E ratio in WACC and in MM 2 computation is made with market values

questions.topic: When growth destroys value, and the ROI the market is pricing
questions.syllabus_objective: DCF valuation: growth, reinvestment and value (g = ROI × CRR); terminal value assumptions
questions.stem: Theta SpA will earn NOPAT of €60m next year. Its WACC is 9% and its net debt is €150m. Management plans to grow NOPAT at 3% a year forever by reinvesting, earning a constant 7.5% return on new investment.

source.file: Slides/Corporate Valuation - AY 26-27 - Lecture 3 - DCF Valuation - v6.pdf
source.label: INFERENCE

subquestions.prompt: Value Theta's enterprise and equity value under its 3% growth plan, and compare the enterprise value with a no-growth policy. Does the plan create value?

The market values Theta's equity at €520m. Assuming the market prices the same 3% growth plan, what return on new investment is it implicitly assuming, and what does that imply about the value of growth?

answer_key.answer: EV 600.0; equity 450.0; no-growth EV 666.7; the plan destroys 66.7 because ROI 7.5% < WACC 9%.
Implied ROI 9.09%, just above the 9% WACC: growth adds only 3.3 of value over no growth.

error_tags.trap: a: NOPAT discounted at WACC − g (EV 1,000)
a: concludes growth adds value
b: market equity used as EV (ROI 6.9%)
b: reinvestment rate reported as ROI

mark_scheme: Second route for [a]: EV = NOPAT × (1 − g/ROI) / (WACC − g) = 60 × 0.6 / 0.06 = 600.0.

[b] Steps: (1) EV = 520 + 150 = 670.0; (2) × (WACC − g): 670.0 × 6% = 40.2; (3) ÷ NOPAT: 0.670 = 1 − g/ROI; (4) g/ROI = 0.330; (5) ROI = 3% / 0.330 = 9.09%; (6) compare with WACC 9%: barely above; (7) value of growth = 670.0 − 666.7 = 3.3, almost nothing.
How to write it: write g = ROI × CRR first, then FCFO = NOPAT × (1 − CRR); state which side of WACC the ROI sits.
Where marks are lost: discounting NOPAT instead of FCFO (EV 1,000), forgetting net debt in [b], or calling any growth value-creating.

citations.quote: If ROI < WACC, an increase in the growth rate decreases value
In the LT, ROI should converge to WACC. This has a powerful consequence: value no longer depends on long term growth
The TV growth rate should not exceed the growth rate of the economy as a whole

questions.topic: Bottom-up beta, synthetic rating and WACC for a private company
questions.syllabus_objective: Cost of capital: CAPM inputs, Blume adjustment, Hamada unlevering and relevering, synthetic rating, WACC
questions.stem: Tau Srl is a private Italian company. Two listed comparables have raw (regression) levered betas and average market D/E ratios of Alfa 1.30 and 0.50, and Beta 1.05 and 0.20; neither is an outlier. Tau's target market D/E is 0.40. The risk-free rate is 3.5% and the market risk premium 5.5%. Tau's EBIT is €40m and its interest expense €12.5m. The Italian statutory corporate income tax rate that allows interest deduction is 24% (the 3.9% regional tax is not on EBT); Tau's effective tax rate last year was 31%. Apply Blume's adjustment to market betas and use the Hamada formula.

source.file: Slides/Corporate Valuation - C31 - Lecture 4 - Cost of Capital - v3.pdf
source.location: slides 7–39 (CAPM, Blume, Hamada, bottom-up beta, tax rate, synthetic rating)
source.label: INFERENCE

subquestions.prompt: Estimate Tau's levered cost of equity with a bottom-up beta. Show each step.
Estimate Tau's cost of debt with a synthetic rating from the slide table and compute its WACC.

answer_key.answer: Blume-adjusted betas 1.200 and 1.033; unlevered 0.870 and 0.897; industry βU 0.883; Tau βL 1.152; kEL 9.83%.
Coverage 3.2× → Ba2/BB, spread 1.8%: kD 5.30%, after tax 4.03%; weights 71.4% equity / 28.6% debt; WACC 8.18%.

error_tags.trap: a: raw betas unlevered directly
a: 31% effective rate instead of the 24% statutory rate
a: book D/E instead of the target market D/E
b: 40% used as the debt weight
b: cost of debt not taxed
b: 27.9% combined rate used

mark_scheme: Second route for [a]: kEU = 3.5% + 0.8833 × 5.5% = 8.358%; add the leverage premium βU × D/E × (1 − t) × MRP = 1.477% → 9.83%.
Where marks are lost: skipping Blume, using the 31% effective or 27.9% combined rate, using D/E (0.40) as the debt weight, or leaving kD pre-tax.
Not needed: the effective tax rate (slides: superficial and prone to mistakes).

citations.quote: the estimated levered ("raw") beta after a number of years tends to converge ("adj") toward 1
Re-lever the industry bU with a reversed Hamada formula
Superficial and prone to mistakes (not directly associated with interest tax shields), but easily applicable

questions.stem: Lambda SpA's balance sheets (€m, end of year) and 2026 income statement are below. The operating tax rate is 28%. Operating cash is needed for daily operations; excess cash is not. Associates are non-consolidated minority stakes. Preferred shares are equity-like claims senior to ordinary shares.

| Operating cash | 10 | 12 |
| Excess cash | 60 | 45 |
| Trade receivables | 150 | 170 |
| Inventory | 120 | 115 |
| Net PP&E | 500 | 540 |
| Investments in associates | 40 | 40 |
| Trade payables | 130 | 150 |
| Employee severance indemnity (TFR) | 30 | 32 |
| Bank loans and bonds | 300 | 330 |
| Preferred shares | 20 | 20 |
| Minority interests | 25 | 27 |

| Income statement 2026 (€m) | |

| Income taxes | (39.8) |
| Net income | 102.2 |

source.file: Slides/Corporate Valuation - C31 - Lecture 5 - Reorganizing and CFs - v13.pdf
source.location: slides 8–28 (reorganised balance sheet, cash flows for valuation, bridge to equity)
source.label: INFERENCE

subquestions.prompt: Reorganise the balance sheets as needed and compute Lambda's FCFO for 2026.
An asset-side DCF values Lambda's operations at €1,400m at the end of 2026. Bridge to the value of the group's ordinary equity and give it per share (40 million shares).

answer_key.answer: NOPAT 115.2; + D&A 60; noncash WC 150 → 147 (releases 3); CAPEX 100.0; FCFO 78.2.
Net debt 285; equity value 1076.0; €26.90 per share.

error_tags.trap: a: excess cash counted as operating
a: D&A not added back to ΔPP&E
a: actual taxes used instead of operating taxes
b: operating cash subtracted in net debt
b: associates left out of the bridge
b: equity-like claims not deducted

mark_scheme: Second route for [a]: core capital employed = NWC + PP&E: 650 → 687 (+37); FCFO = NOPAT − ΔCE = 115.2 − 37 = 78.2.

[b] Steps: (1) gross debt 330; (2) net debt = 330 − excess cash 45 = 285 (operating cash stays in WC); (3) + associates 40; (4) − TFR 32 (debt-like); (5) − minorities 27; (6) − preferred 20; (7) equity = 1,400 − 285 + 40 − 32 − 27 − 20 = 1076.0; (8) per share = 1076.0 / 40 = €26.90.
Where marks are lost: counting excess cash as operating, CAPEX = ΔPP&E only (40), operating taxes on EBT, deducting operating cash, forgetting associates, minorities or preferred shares.
Not needed in [a]: interest and reported income taxes (FCFO uses operating taxes on EBIT).

citations.quote: The "non-cash (or non-debt) working capital" for valuation only includes the assets and the liabilities with an operating nature
"Pensions": employee termination indemnities
FCFO = NOPAT - increase in core capital employed during the year
Moving from EV to EqV and vice-versa requires the "bridge" of other remaining balance sheet items

questions.topic: FCFO from EBITDA, then a two-stage DCF at the right valuation date
questions.syllabus_objective: DCF exercises: building FCFO, two-stage asset-side DCF, valuation date, bridge to equity
questions.stem: Mu SpA reports for 2027 (€m): EBITDA 260; D&A 60; new investments 90; disposals of fixed assets 10 (sold at book value, so no gain or loss); noncash working capital 70 at end-2026 and 85 at end-2027; interest 14; debt rose from 380 to 400. Tax rate 25%.

source.file: Slides/Corporate Valuation - C31 - Lecture 6 - DCF Exercises - v1.pdf
source.location: L6 problems 2.5 (FCFO) and 4.1 (valuation date); L3 slide 18 (two-stage model)
source.label: INFERENCE

subquestions.prompt: Plan FCFO is €125m in 2028 and €132m in 2029, growing 2% a year from 2030. WACC is 9% and net debt at the end of 2027 is €400m. What are Mu's enterprise and equity values on 31/12/2027?

answer_key.answer: EBIT 200; NOPAT 150; + D&A 60; − net investments 80; − ΔNWC 15; FCFO 115.0.

error_tags.trap: a: gross investments of 90 deducted
a: NWC increase added
a: interest or debt flows in FCFO
b: 2027 FCFO counted although it is already paid
b: terminal value discounted one year too many
b: TV = FCFO 2029 / (WACC − g)

mark_scheme: [a] Steps: (1) EBIT = 260 − 60 = 200; (2) operating taxes 25% = 50; (3) NOPAT = 150; (4) + D&A 60; (5) net investment = 90 − 10 = 80; (6) ΔNWC = 85 − 70 = +15 absorbs cash; (7) FCFO = 150 + 60 − 80 − 15 = 115.0.
Second route for [a]: EBITDA × (1 − t) + D&A × t − 80 − 15 = 195 + 15 − 95 = 115.0.
Second route for [b]: roll back: value at end-2028 = (132 + 1923.43) / 1.09 = 1885.71; EV = (125 + that) / 1.09 = 1844.7.

Where marks are lost: deducting gross investments, adding the NWC increase, putting interest or debt changes in FCFO, including 2027's flow, discounting the TV three years, or not growing FCFO 2029 into the TV.
Not needed: interest and the change in debt (they belong to FCFE, not FCFO).

citations.quote: How much is the company’s FCFO for valuation purposes in 2019?
What is the enterprise value as of 31/12/2016?
a second subsequent stage (the terminal value), with a constant growth assumption
